doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Daily life and virtual studio work during lockdown
summary: He fills CD orders, plays virtual concerts, records guitar parts remotely, now with video, and works on arrangements for a musical in development.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: It looks like California was doing the right thing and now seems to be going backwards. What’s your day to day life like? Do you go out much?

I go to the post office to fill orders for CDs when they come in. We were getting out more, we’ve actually kind of scaled back because I think California’s going to go back into full lockdown sometime in the next week or so. So, one second. Excuse me. But I mean I’ve done a few, I did a virtual concert from a local theater last month. I played at a © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

virtual gala where I drove down to San Diego. I mean I’ve done a few gigs. I’ve done a few sessions, like socially distant sessions where everybody is isolated. But mostly I feel like I’m going back to an earlier era before I really started putting out solo guitar records and touring, when I was active as a composer doing T.V. and movie stuff. And so, and there’s a musical that we have that is in development that we were anticipating a tour later this year that’s now pushed back into next year. So I’ve been working on arrangements and demos for that, and doing kind of virtual studio work. People send me tracks to do guitar parts. But the one thing that’s quite different these days is that whereas it used to be I’d just send an audio track, now they want video too. And that’s a little different scenario because whereas if you’re building a guitar track for example you can do it a phrase at a time or a section at a time. Hang on one sec — you can do it one section at a time, but when you’re doing like performance video, if they want a performance out of it you actually have to perform the piece you know, and it’s a little different approach to the way of recording things. Right now I’m doing something for, there’s an L.A. film conducting intensive where they assigned composers to write pieces for various instruments. And they asked me to be the guitar player to interpret this, and I just got sent three pieces that I’ve got to record and video myself doing, one of those, this week. And I’ve identified the one that is the most guitaristic, but there’s another one that’s kind of a cool electric guitar thing that requires either looping or overdubs. So I may end up just recording that on its own terms. Because it seems like an interesting composition. But there are that kind of thing where it’s like okay give us an iPhone video. Well you know I’m set up here to do a higher level of recording than that, so I might use the iPhone for like a fourth camera if I want to do multiple cameras. So I’ve had to become a bit conversant with the video and streaming technology just to be able to stay on top a bit. And you know it’s no longer being able to kind of fall out of bed, grab a cup of tea and then come into the studio. You know you’ve got to coif the ‘do. And there are certain periods of day in here where I have stained glass windows kind of either side, and the light comes in. And yesterday I did something for a Beatle-related project where I kind of timed it so that the light was shining on my fingers so I’d kind of go to a particular chord and there would be this kind of flash of light. And it was kind of like, it was a cool effect. So I hope they like it ‘cause it was fun to do.
Speaking of effects, I’m going to just alter our view here for a moment. It sounds like you’re about as busy as you could be.
That’s great. Did you have a time back, I don’t know, maybe in March or something, a certain moment where you really started to believe that this pandemic was serious? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
